title: Ἀνὴρ ⟨δηχθεὶς ὑπὸ μύρμηκος⟩ καὶ Ἑρμῆς
titleEn: The Man Bitten by an Ant, and Hermes
part: The Man Bitten by an Ant, and Hermes (Chambry 48 · Perry 306)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 48 (= Perry 306). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ναῦν ποτε μετὰ τῶν ἀνδρῶν βυθισθεῖσαν ἰδών τις ἀδίκως ἔλεγε τοὺς θεοὺς κρίνειν· δι’ ἕνα γὰρ ἀσεβῆ συναπώλοντο καὶ ἀναίτιοι.
sentences.tr: Naun pote meta tōn andrōn bythistheisan idōn tis adikōs elege tous theous krinein· di' hena gar asebē synapōlonto kai anaitioi.
sentences.l: Someone, having-seen a ship once sunk together with its men, was saying that the gods judge unjustly; for because of one impious man the guiltless too had perished along with him.
sentences.i: A man who had seen a ship go down with everyone aboard said that the gods judged unjustly: because of one impious man the innocent had perished along with him.
sentences.n: ἔλεγε … κρίνειν is accusative and infinitive after a verb of saying, 'said that the gods judge'. The γάρ clause is his reason, given in his own voice; the whole complaint sits in the σύν- of συναπώλοντο, 'they perished along with him'. Chambry's title supplies ⟨δηχθεὶς ὑπὸ μύρμηκος⟩ in angle brackets — the editor's words, not the manuscripts'.

sentences.t: Ταῦτα αὐτοῦ λέγοντος, μυρμήκων πολλῶν ὄντων ἐν τῷ τόπῳ ἐν ᾧ ἔτυχεν ἱστάμενος, συνέβη ὑφ’ ἑνὸς δηχθῆναι τοῦτον.
sentences.tr: Tauta autou legontos, myrmēkōn pollōn ontōn en tōi topōi en hōi etychen histamenos, synebē hyph' henos dēchthēnai touton.
sentences.l: As he was saying these things, there being many ants in the place in which he happened to be standing, it came about that he was bitten by one of them.
sentences.i: While he was saying this — there were a great many ants in the spot where he happened to be standing — it came about that one of them bit him.
sentences.n: Two genitive absolutes stacked one on the other (ταῦτα αὐτοῦ λέγοντος, μυρμήκων … ὄντων), then συνέβη with an infinitive, 'it came about that…'. ἔτυχεν ἱστάμενος is τυγχάνω with the supplementary participle again; ὑφ' ἑνός is ὑπό with the genitive for the agent.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ὑφ’ ἑνὸς δηχθεὶς συνεπάτησε τοὺς πάντας.
sentences.tr: Ho de hyph' henos dēchtheis synepatēse tous pantas.
sentences.l: And he, bitten by one, trampled them all underfoot.
sentences.n: ὑφ’ ἑνὸς δηχθείς picks up ὑφ’ ἑνὸς δηχθῆναι from the sentence before, the same words with the infinitive turned into a participle, and that repetition is the whole argument: bitten by one, he destroys the lot — the very thing he has just charged the gods with.

sentences.t: Ἑρμῆς δὲ ἐπιστὰς αὐτῷ καὶ τῇ ῥάβδῳ παίων εἶπεν· « Εἶτα οὐκ ἀνέχῃ σὺ τοὺς θεοὺς δικαστὰς εἶναι οἷος εἶ σὺ τῶν μυρμήκων ; »
sentences.tr: Hermēs de epistas autōi kai tēi rhabdōi paiōn eipen· « Eita ouk anechēi sy tous theous dikastas einai hoios ei sy tōn myrmēkōn ; »
sentences.l: And Hermes, having-stood-over him and striking him with his staff, said: « So then, do you not put up with the gods being judges such as you are of the ants? »
sentences.i: Then Hermes stood over him and, striking him with his staff, said: « So you will not have the gods for judges of the same sort that you are to the ants? »
sentences.n: The ῥάβδος is Hermes' wand, the rod he carries in Homer to charm eyes asleep and to marshal the dead; it is often drawn together with the herald's staff, the κηρύκειον, though the words are not the same. ἐπιστάς, 'having taken his stand over him', is the regular word for a god's sudden arrival beside a mortal — often in a dream. In οἷος εἶ σὺ τῶν μυρμήκων the noun δικαστής is carried over from the clause before: 'such (a judge) as you are of the ants'.

sentences.t: Ὅτι μηδεὶς θεοῦ βλασφημείτω, συμφορᾶς ἐπελθούσης, μᾶλλον δὲ σκοπείτω τὰς οἰκείας ἁμαρτίας.
sentences.tr: Hoti mēdeis theou blasphēmeitō, symphoras epelthousēs, mallon de skopeitō tas oikeias hamartias.
sentences.l: That: let no one speak ill of a god, misfortune having come upon him, but rather let him look at his own faults.
sentences.i: The story shows that no one should revile a god when calamity comes, but should look instead at his own faults.
sentences.n: A bare Ὅτι moral: the 'the story shows' is unexpressed in the Greek, which opens simply 'That…', and is supplied in the idiomatic line. βλασφημείτω and σκοπείτω are third-person imperatives, Greek's way of laying down a rule — 'let him…'. συμφορᾶς ἐπελθούσης is one more genitive absolute; θεοῦ with βλασφημείτω is a genitive of the one reviled.
